body.name: Accenture
rounds: Cognitive and technical assessment
Coding assessment
Communication assessment (spoken English)
Interview (technical and HR together)
questions: Tell me about yourself.
Tell me about a time you worked in a team to meet a deadline.
What do you know about Accenture?
How do you keep learning new technologies?
Tell me about a time a plan changed suddenly and you had to adapt.
Tell me about a time you helped someone from a different background feel included in a team.
Tell me about a time you did more than you were asked to make a customer or user happy.
Explain cloud computing to a client who has never used it, and name one risk they should know about.
What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases, and when would you choose each?
A client says their shopping website is down during a big sale. What are your first steps?
How would you estimate how many people in Bengaluru order food through an app in a week?
For experienced candidates: tell me about a project where you moved a client's system to the cloud or a new platform. What went wrong?
Why do you want to work in consulting and technology services rather than at a product company?
Do you have any questions for us?
tips: Speak clearly and at an even pace: there's a separate spoken-English test.
Read Accenture's recent work in your area before the interview.
In the communication test, listen to the whole prompt before answering and keep your sentences short and complete.
Practise coding problems under time in the language you'll choose, including reading input and printing output correctly.
Prepare stories on teamwork, deadlines and adapting to change; the single interview mixes them with technical questions.

body.name: Adobe
rounds: Online application, often with a portfolio or GitHub link for technical and creative roles
Call with a Talent Partner about the role and your interest in Adobe
Online coding test or technical screen for many engineering and campus roles
Interview with the hiring manager on past work and measurable impact
Skills assessments and team interviews: coding, system design or portfolio review; creative briefs or case studies for creative roles
looks_for: Measurable impact from your past work
Strong fundamentals for engineering roles: data structures, algorithms, OS and object-oriented design
Care for the creators, businesses and document users who rely on Adobe's products
questions: Tell me about a time you owned an outcome from start to finish, including the parts nobody asked you to do.
Tell me about a time you raised the quality bar on your team's work. What did you change?
Tell me about a time you were candid that something wasn't working.
Tell me about a project where you used AI tools to improve your work. What did you do yourself, and what did you check?
Tell me about a time you got something wrong in a project. How did you put it right?
How would you design undo and redo for an image editor?
How would you let two people edit the same design file at the same time?
How would you make a web app open very large PDF files quickly?
Explain the difference between stack and heap memory in C++, and how the choice affects performance and safety.
A user says a filter in a desktop app gives different colours on Windows and macOS. How would you investigate?
How would you help a first-time user get a good result in a design app within their first five minutes?
How would you tell whether free trials are turning into paid subscriptions, and what would you try to improve it?
Why Adobe? Which Adobe product do you use, and what would you change about it?
Which of Adobe's values fits you best, and when have you lived it?
tips: Have a specific 'Why Adobe?' answer ready, tied to a product you actually use and the team you're interviewing for.
Add a portfolio or GitHub link to your application; Adobe's hiring page suggests it for technical and creative roles.
Prepare examples with measurable impact for the hiring manager interview; Adobe's hiring page asks for them.
Adobe asks candidates not to use AI recording, live-scribing or conversation-prompting tools in hiring conversations unless invited, and to show how they've used AI in their work instead.
For C++, graphics or imaging teams, revise memory management, multithreading and basic image processing.
For product or design roles, practise a short case presentation: the user, the problem, your options and why you chose one.

body.name: Airbnb
rounds: Recruiter call
Technical or craft screen (for engineers, often a live coding interview)

Clean, working code and clear communication
questions: Tell me about a time you went out of your way to make someone feel welcome or supported at work.
Tell me about a time you turned a bold idea into something real with limited resources.
Tell me about a setback you bounced back from. What did it teach you?
Tell me about a time you had to build trust between two groups who wanted different things.

How would you support many languages and currencies in one app?

What does belonging mean to you, at work or when you travel?
tips: Prepare true, personal stories for the core values interviews; candidates commonly describe them as conversations about who you are, not only your work.
Use the product as a guest and read how hosting works, so you can talk about both sides of the marketplace.
In coding rounds, aim for code that runs and talk through edge cases as you go.
Read your interview invitation carefully: Airbnb's careers FAQ says some roles involve a test, a video or an event.

body.name: Apple
rounds: Recruiter screen
One or two phone or video interviews with the team
Onsite or virtual loop with several team members, often including the hiring manager
questions: Tell me about a product you love and what you'd change about it.
Walk me through the work you're proudest of, in detail.
Tell me about a time you pushed back on a decision because quality would suffer.
Tell me about a time you worked closely with another discipline, such as design or hardware, to ship something.

body.name: Atlassian
rounds: Recruiter screen
Technical interviews: coding and system design
A values interview
Hiring manager / management interview
looks_for: Clear reasoning about trade-offs in code and design
How you collaborate and communicate, including with people outside engineering
questions: Tell me about a time you shared bad news openly.
Tell me about a time you balanced speed with doing it right.
Tell me about something you changed for the better at work.
Tell me about a time a customer problem made you change your team's plans.
Tell me about a team success you're proud of. How did you help others do their best work?
Tell me about working with teammates in other time zones. How did you keep work visible and decisions clear?
How would you design notifications for an issue tracker like Jira, so people hear about changes that matter without being flooded?
Talk me through how you'd design a shared page editor where several people can edit the same page at once.
Walk me through how you'd structure the code for a simple rate limiter so it's easy to change and test.
Walk me through a past project: who you worked with, the hardest technical problem and the business reason for the work.
A release you shipped has broken a feature for a large customer. What do you do in the first hour, and afterwards?
Why Atlassian? Which of its products have you used, and what would you improve in one?
Which Atlassian value means most to you, and when have you acted on it?
tips: The values interview carries real weight: prepare a story for each value.
Atlassian's engineering guide says interviewers care more about how you reason through trade-offs than about a missing line of code, so talk through your choices.
The coding interview covers code design as well as data structures: think about naming, structure and how you'd test what you write.
In system design, ask about users, reliability and cost before drawing boxes, and expect follow-ups that change the constraints.
Values interviewers often come from outside engineering, so keep stories free of jargon. Credit your team, then be clear about your own part.
In the manager interview, say so if you don't know something; Atlassian's own guide recommends it.

body.name: Bain & Company
rounds: Application review, sometimes with a recruiter call
Digital assessment for many consulting roles: problem solving, communication and analytical skills
First round: case interviews plus questions on your experience
Final round: more case and behavioural interviews, often with senior team members
For non-consulting roles: a coding challenge, portfolio walkthrough or written assignment instead of a case (varies)
looks_for: True North: doing the right thing by clients, people and communities
Curiosity and a love of solving problems
Focus on results for clients, not just analysis
questions: Tell me about yourself and walk me through your CV.
Tell me about a time you were open about a mistake or problem when it would have been easier to stay quiet.
Tell me about a time you helped a teammate succeed, even though it wasn't your job.
Tell me about a time you chose a practical solution over a perfect one. Was it the right call?
Describe something you committed to and saw through despite setbacks.
A private equity firm is thinking of buying a chain of dental clinics. What would you want to know before advising it?
A sports shoe brand's profits fell while its sales stayed flat. How would you structure the problem?
A food delivery company wants to launch in a new city. How would you decide whether it's worth it?
Estimate how many hair salons there are in Bengaluru.
Quick maths: if a product's price rises 10% and the volume sold falls 5%, what happens to revenue?
Your analysis points one way, but the client's chief executive strongly believes the opposite. How would you handle the next meeting?
Why Bain, and what do you know about how it works with clients?
Which industry or type of problem would you most like to work on, and why?
tips: Bain says there isn't necessarily one right answer in a case; it watches how you structure the problem and build on ideas as the case moves.
Don't force a memorised framework; adapt your structure to the problem this client faces and say why.
Practise mental maths: percentages, growth rates and break-even, without a calculator.
Practise cases out loud with a partner and reflect on the feedback after each one, rather than cramming at the end.
Bain's careers site says it never interviews over instant messaging and never asks candidates to pay; treat messages like that as a warning sign.

body.name: BCG
rounds: Online application, with an online test or online case for some offices and roles
Skills interview on your experience, skills and motivation
Case interviews: a realistic business problem worked through with the interviewer
Team interview for client-facing roles, again on problem solving, analysis and communication
looks_for: Structuring a problem and stating assumptions
Quick, accurate calculations and reading data
Clear communication and a summary that ends in a recommendation
questions: Tell me about yourself and what brings you to consulting.
Tell me about a time curiosity made you dig further into a problem than you needed to.
Tell me about a time you came up with an unusual solution to a problem.
Describe a time you helped a team work better together.
Tell me about the achievement you're proudest of. What drove you?
A coffee chain's new stores are less profitable than its older ones. How would you find out why?
A car maker is deciding whether to launch a subscription service for its electric cars. How would you assess it?
Estimate the yearly demand for school notebooks in Bengaluru. Talk me through your assumptions.

A software company can enter one of three new countries first. How would you decide which?

Why BCG, and why consulting?
What would you want to learn in your first year here, and how would you know you're growing?

Don't force a memorised framework onto the case; build a structure for the specific problem in front of you.
If the interviewer nudges you mid-case, take it, adjust, and say how it changes your thinking.
Prepare a story for each quality BCG lists: integrity, curiosity, creative thinking, collaboration and drive.
BCG offers a free job simulation, OneDay@BCG, on its careers site; it's a useful way to see the kind of work cases are based on.
Practise mental maths with percentages and growth rates, and round sensibly as you go.

body.name: BrowserStack

Hiring manager round
Culture or values conversation

Working well in a remote-first team

body.name: Cisco

Collaboration, which Cisco's careers site calls how it gets things done
Your own thinking and experience, not scripted answers
Coding and problem solving for software roles
Security awareness in how you design and run systems

What questions do you have for us about the team or the role?

body.name: Citi

Clear problem solving in technical or case questions

Tell me about a time you spotted a risk early. What did you do?

Why Citi, and why this programme?
Where do you want to be in five years, and how would this role help you get there?

body.name: Coforge

Why Coforge?

Revise SQL and testing basics; they come up across development and support roles.
If you mention a technology, be ready to describe one thing you built or fixed with it.
Read a recent Coforge press release or case study so 'why Coforge' is specific.

body.name: Cognizant
rounds: Online assessment (aptitude and coding)
Technical interview
HR interview

body.name: Concentrix
rounds: Online application, walk-in or recruitment drive

Recruiter or HR interview
Operations interview, sometimes with a short mock customer call

Typing and note-taking accuracy while you talk
Reliability with attendance, shifts and schedules

body.name: CRED
rounds: Recruiter or hiring team screen
Problem-solving / data structures round
Machine coding or low-level design round (for many engineering roles)

Hiring manager and culture conversation

Reference conversations, then an offer

body.name: Delhivery

Technical rounds on problem-solving, data and your projects
System design for experienced engineers
Case or operations round for supply chain, analytics and business roles

Describe a time you held yourself or your team to a higher standard than anyone asked for.
Tell me about a time you put a team win ahead of getting credit yourself.
Tell me about a bold change you proposed. How did you get people behind it?
How would you design a help desk system that routes each support ticket to the right agent?
What does multi-tenancy mean in a SaaS product, and how would you keep one customer's data safe from another's?
How would you build service-level timers for support tickets that pause outside business hours and on holidays?
A large customer says your product became slow after the last release. What would you do?
How would you design public APIs and webhooks so customers can connect your product to their other tools?
A customer on a yearly plan uses only a small part of the product, and renewal is three months away. What would you do?

Which Freshworks value do you relate to most, and when have you lived it?

In design rounds, think in tenants: which data belongs to which customer, and how one heavy customer can't slow down the rest.
For sales and customer success roles, practise explaining a product's value in the customer's words, not as a list of features.

body.name: Genpact
rounds: Online application, walk-in or campus drive
Online assessment for many entry-level roles: aptitude and English, with domain or typing questions for some
HR or recruiter interview
Operations, functional or technical interview with the hiring team
For analytics and technology roles: a technical round on SQL, Excel or coding
Final discussion with a manager (some roles)
looks_for: Accuracy and attention to detail with numbers and processes
Clear written and spoken English with clients
Excel and basic accounting for finance roles; SQL for analytics roles
Comfort with process discipline, deadlines and service levels
questions: Tell me about yourself.
Tell me about a time you asked 'why' and found a better way to do a routine task.
Tell me about a time you spoke up about a problem when it would have been easier to stay quiet.
Tell me about a time you cut through a lot of information to find the one thing that mattered.
Tell me about a time you made an error with numbers or data. How did you catch it and fix it?
Explain the difference between accounts payable and accounts receivable.
What does a lookup function such as VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP do, and when would a pivot table be better?
You find an invoice that doesn't match its purchase order. What do you do?
A process your team runs misses its turnaround target most Mondays. How would you find out why?
For analytics roles: how would you find customers who haven't ordered in the last 90 days using SQL? Talk me through it.
A client emails angrily about a delayed report. How would you reply?

Why Genpact, and why this kind of role?
Are you comfortable working night shifts or hours that follow a client's time zone?
Do you have any questions for us?

In the English assessment and the HR round, answer in short, complete sentences and check you've understood the question first.
For process roles, show you care about accuracy and deadlines with an example that has a number.
Recent graduates in India may also see Genpact's apprenticeship programme: it's a training scheme, and a full-time role afterwards depends on business needs.

body.name: Goldman Sachs
rounds: Online assessment (coding, maths, aptitude)
Technical interviews: data structures, problem solving
'Superday': several back-to-back interviews including behavioral and fit
questions: Tell me about a time you worked under real pressure. What did you do?
Why Goldman Sachs, and why this division?
Tell me about a mistake you caught before it reached anyone else.
Tell me about a time you depended on others to hit a deadline. How did you keep the team on track?
Tell me about a time you went beyond what a client, user or professor expected.
Walk me through the three financial statements and how they link together.
How would you value a company? Explain the main approaches and when you'd prefer each.
If interest rates rise sharply, what happens to bond prices, and why?

Tell me about a recent market move or deal you followed. Why did it happen, and who did it affect?
How would you design a system that shows traders live prices for thousands of instruments with very little delay?
Explain the difference between a process and a thread, and a problem you've seen from shared state.
You roll two fair dice. What's the chance the total is at least 10? Talk me through it.
Where do you see yourself in five years, and how does this role get you there?

Know why this division specifically, not just why finance.

For engineering roles, practise explaining your approach to a coding problem and its time and space cost out loud before you write code.

Read the financial news for a few weeks before; be ready to discuss one market move and one company in depth.

body.name: Google
rounds: Recruiter call
One or two technical phone screens (coding in a shared doc)
Onsite or virtual loop: coding, system design (for experienced roles), and a 'Googleyness and leadership' interview
Hiring committee review
looks_for: General cognitive ability: how you reason through an open problem
Googleyness: comfort with ambiguity, collaboration, doing the right thing
questions: Tell me about a time you had to work through a problem with no clear owner or direction.
How would you estimate how many people use Google Maps on a weekday morning in Bengaluru?
Tell me about a time you helped a teammate who was struggling.
Walk me through the hardest technical decision you've made and the trade-offs you weighed.
Tell me about a time you changed your mind after getting new information.
Tell me about a time you led something without having any formal authority.
How would you design a service that suggests search queries as someone types?
A web page loads slowly for some users but not for others. How would you find out why?
How would you remove duplicates from a list too large to fit in memory? Talk me through the trade-offs.

Why Google, and which product or team would you most like to work on?
Which Google product do you use most, and what would you change about it?
Where do you want your career to be in a few years, and how would this role help?

For coding, talk through complexity and edge cases before you write.

For the Googleyness and leadership interview, prepare stories about ambiguity, helping others and leading without a title.
Google says it scores structured interviews against rubrics, so answer the question you were asked fully before adding extras.

body.name: Groww
rounds: Application directly or through a referral
Screening call about you, the role and your goals
Team interviews on skills: coding and problem-solving for engineers, cases or functional depth for other roles
System design for experienced engineering roles (often)
Hiring manager or leadership conversation, often on ownership and customer focus
Offer; the careers page says Groww aims to move fast and reply within days
looks_for: Transparency by default: sharing context openly across teams
Stepping outside your role to help the team (the careers page says a role is "a starting point, not a fence")
Building reliable, correct systems for a very large base of retail investors
questions: Tell me about a time you made something simpler for a user who wasn't an expert.
Tell me about a decision where doing right by the customer cost you something in the short term.
Describe a time you helped another team with a problem that wasn't yours.
Tell me about an experiment or idea you tried that didn't work. What did you learn and change?
How would you design the system behind a monthly SIP that invests automatically? What can go wrong?
When a popular IPO opens, traffic to one page jumps sharply. How would you keep the app responsive?
Explain idempotency and why it matters when a user taps "Buy" twice on a slow network.
Many new users sign up but never make their first investment. How would you find out why, and what would you try?
How would you explain the difference between a direct and a regular mutual fund plan to a first-time investor?
A customer says money has left their bank account but the investment doesn't show in the app. How would you handle it?
What metrics would you track to know whether a new stock screener is helping users?
How would you design alerts for unusual login or trading activity on an account without annoying genuine users?
Why Groww? Which of its values do you connect with most, and when have you shown it?
What would you change in the Groww app, and how would you test whether it helped?
tips: Use the Groww app before the interview: browse a fund and a stock page, try the screens a beginner would, and note one thing you'd simplify.
Tie answers to the three published values; Simple is Beautiful is a natural lens for product and design questions.
For engineering, talk about correctness and failure: duplicate taps, partial payments, and traffic peaks at market open.
Know basic investing terms (SIP, NAV, demat, KYC, F&O) well enough to explain them in plain words.
Expect follow-ups that check whether you'd stay honest with customers when it's inconvenient.

body.name: HCLTech
rounds: Online application or campus registration, then shortlisting
Online assessment for many fresher drives: aptitude, reasoning, English and coding or technical questions
Technical interview on fundamentals and your projects; puzzles or problem-solving questions are possible
Managerial or client interview (for many experienced roles)
HR interview on goals, strengths and flexibility
looks_for: Programming, database and networking basics, explained simply
Calm reasoning on puzzles and unfamiliar problems
Hands-on knowledge of everything on your resume
Willingness to learn new platforms, from cloud to infrastructure tools
questions: Walk me through your background and why you applied to HCLTech.
Tell me about a time you solved a problem nobody had shown you how to solve.
Tell me about a time you made sure everyone in a team was heard, including quieter members.
Describe a time you chose to do the right thing when a shortcut was available.
Tell me about critical feedback you received on your work. What did you change?
What is the difference between TCP and UDP, and where is each used?
A server's disk is suddenly full and an application has stopped. How would you find what filled it?
What is virtualisation, and how does it relate to cloud computing?
Talk me through how you'd find duplicate records in a table using SQL.
How would you estimate how many laptops an office of a large company in Bengaluru replaces each year?
A user says an application works on a colleague's laptop but not on theirs. How would you troubleshoot it?
For experienced candidates: walk me through how an incident is handled on your project, from alert to closure.
Why HCLTech, and which part of its business interests you most?
Are you comfortable with shift work or support roles at the start of your career?
What would you like to learn in your first year here?
tips: HCLTech's careers site says interview questions may include puzzles; think aloud, state your assumptions and check your answer.
Revise networking and operating-system basics as well as coding: many roles are in infrastructure and support.
Know every tool on your resume well enough to describe one task you did with it.
Have a clear, honest answer on shifts and the kind of work you're open to before the HR round.
Read about HCLTech's main businesses (IT and business services, engineering and R&D services, HCLSoftware) so 'why HCLTech' is specific.

body.name: HDFC Bank
rounds: Application through the careers site, a campus drive or a recruitment programme for some roles
Online aptitude test for many entry-level and programme roles, often covering reasoning, numbers, English and banking awareness
Interview with the hiring manager or a panel on your background, banking awareness and communication
For sales and relationship roles, often a role play or questions on handling customers and targets
HR discussion on fit, location and joining
Document and background checks before joining
looks_for: Comfort with sales targets and building customer relationships
Basic banking awareness: accounts, loans, interest rates and the RBI's role
Accuracy, compliance and honesty when handling customers' money
Willingness to work in different branches or cities
questions: Tell me about a time you convinced someone to try something new: a product, an idea or a change.
Describe a time you handled an upset customer or member of the public.
Tell me about a time you were at risk of missing a target or deadline. What did you do?
Tell me about a time you caught an error in a document or calculation before it caused a problem.
A customer has a large balance in a savings account and no plan for it. How would you approach the conversation?
What is the repo rate, and how does a change in it affect a bank's loans and deposits?
What is KYC, and why must a bank complete it before opening an account?
How would you offer a credit card to a customer who says they don't want any debt?
What is a non-performing asset, and why do banks watch them closely?

Explain how a UPI payment moves from one bank account to another.

Why HDFC Bank, and why banking as a career?
Are you comfortable working to a sales target and being posted to any branch or city?

Read the bank's recent press releases and RBI announcements so you can talk about current banking news.
Apply only through official channels; a request to pay money for an interview or offer letter is a warning sign of fraud.
Prepare a short, calm explanation for any gap year or change of stream.

body.name: Hexaware
rounds: Campus drive, off-campus registration or online application
Online assessment for many fresher drives: aptitude, English and coding
Technical interview on fundamentals, testing or cloud basics, and your projects
For experienced roles: a second technical or managerial round
HR interview
looks_for: Interest in automation and cloud work
questions: Tell me about yourself.
Tell me about a time you put a teammate's needs ahead of your own plan.
Tell me about a time you automated or simplified a repetitive task.
Tell me about a time you made someone new feel welcome in a team or group.
Tell me about a time you missed a deadline. What did you change afterwards?
What is the difference between manual and automated testing, and when is automation worth it?
Explain the difference between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, with an example of each.

Why Hexaware?

Do you have any questions for us?

Revise SQL joins and basic testing terms; they come up across development and testing roles.
Read about the Mavericks graduate programme before the HR round so you can say what you want from it.

body.name: HSBC
rounds: Short online application with eligibility questions and, for some roles, a CV
Online assessments of cognitive and behavioural skills; technology programmes add a coding assessment
Video interview for some roles, live or recorded without an interviewer
Interview or assessment centre (a 'Super Day' in the US), often around three hours with exercises and team interviews

looks_for: A clear reason for choosing HSBC, the industry and the business area
Specific examples: the situation, your task, what you did and the result
Care for customers and for doing things the right way in a regulated business

Describe a time you worked with people in another team, country or time zone to deliver something.

HSBC's guidance allows AI tools for preparing, such as practising answers, but not for generating responses during live or recorded interviews.

body.name: IBM

Technical interview
Manager / HR interview

Results you can quantify: the share of a target you achieved, and in what time
Leadership early in your career, such as leading a university team project
questions: Tell me about a team project you led. How did you take responsibility for the outcome?
Tell me about a target you were given and how you met it. Put numbers on it.
Describe a time you solved a problem for a customer that wasn't strictly your job.
Tell me about a time you worked with people from very different teams to get something done.
Explain how a mobile data session reaches the internet, from the phone to the core network.
What changes from 4G to 5G, and what does it mean for users and for the network team?
Customers in one area complain about slow mobile data every evening. How would you investigate?
How would you plan a fibre broadband rollout in a new residential area of Pune?
How would you grow sales of a new prepaid plan in a small town where most people already have a SIM?
Explain the difference between TCP and UDP, and where each fits in a video call.
A store's daily activations have dropped suddenly. What would you check first?
Why Jio? Which of its six values do you relate to most, and when have you shown it?
Are you open to working in any city, or in field roles, if the business needs it?
What would you like to ask us about the role or about Jio?

Revise telecom basics for technical roles: spectrum, radio access and core network, fibre, latency and capacity.
Prepare for an aptitude test as well as interviews: practise basic maths and logical reasoning for speed.
Prepare thoughtful questions; Jio's How We Hire page says they show your understanding and interest.

body.name: JPMorgan Chase
rounds: Online application and assessments
Recorded video interview (HireVue)
'Superday' of back-to-back interviews, technical and behavioral
looks_for: A commitment to integrity, fairness and responsibility
A great team and winning culture
questions: Why JPMorgan, and why this business?
Tell me about a time you worked under pressure.
Tell me about a time you made a mistake. How did you fix it?
Tell me about a time you put a customer's or user's needs first, even though it cost you time.
Tell me about a time you improved a process so it ran faster or with fewer errors.
Tell me about a time you did the right thing when an easier option was available.
What's the difference between investment banking, commercial banking and asset management?
Explain how a rise in interest rates affects a bank's lending business and its customers.
Explain, step by step, what happens when someone pays by card in a shop.
A small-business customer says a new online banking feature is confusing. How would you work out what to fix first?
How would you design a service that alerts customers about unusual transactions on their accounts?
You've inherited code with no tests, and it must change before a big release. How would you approach it safely?
What do you know about the business you're applying to, and how does it make money?
tips: Practise recorded answers: the video round is timed and has no interviewer.
Know the business line you're applying to.
In the recorded round, look at the camera, answer in about a minute and finish on the result; practise with a timer.
Use numbers when you describe what you achieved; the firm's careers site asks candidates to show results with measurable data.
For technology roles, be ready to explain a project's design choices and how you tested it, not only what it does.
Learn the firm's main businesses and say clearly which one you want and why.

body.name: KPMG
rounds: Online assessment: comprehension, reasoning and psychometric questions (quantitative or data questions for some practices)
Group discussion (some campus roles)
Case study round, written or as a discussion
Interview with a recruiter on fit and behaviour
Technical panel interview, sometimes with two or three interviewers
looks_for: Integrity: we do what is right
Excellence: we never stop learning and improving
Courage: we think and act boldly
Together: we respect each other and draw strength from our differences
For Better: we do what matters
questions: Tell me about yourself and why you're interested in professional services.
Tell me about a time you did the right thing when it would have been easier not to.
Tell me about a time you taught yourself something difficult so you could do better work.
Describe a time you suggested a bold idea. How did people react, and what happened?
Tell me about a time you worked closely with someone very different from you to get a result.
What is materiality in an audit, and how does it change what an auditor tests?
A client's inventory records don't match the warehouse count. How would you investigate?
Explain transfer pricing in simple terms, and why tax authorities care about it.
How would you assess whether a mid-sized company is ready to move to a new ERP system?
A bank wants fewer false alarms from its anti-money-laundering checks without missing real cases. How would you approach it?
A retail chain's sales grew this year but its profit stayed flat. Where would you look?
Why KPMG, and why this practice?
Where do you see yourself in five years, and are you planning a professional qualification?
tips: Practise reading a short business case and summarising it in a minute: the problem, the key facts, and what you'd recommend.
In a case round, state your structure first, then go area by area, saying your assumptions as you go.
For the technical panel, revise your subject's basics, such as accounting standards, tax or the tools on your CV, and be ready to apply them to an example.
In the group discussion, make two or three structured points, build on others' points rather than talking over them, and offer to summarise at the end.
Keep behavioural answers short: the situation, what you did, and the result, with a number if you can.
Read about one recent change in your field, such as a new accounting rule, a tax change or a technology trend, and what it means for clients.

body.name: Larsen & Toubro
rounds: Campus shortlisting, or an online application for some programmes
Online test of domain knowledge and cognitive aptitude (for GETs, per L&T's careers site)
A one-on-one interview, usually covering core subjects, projects and fit
Health examination before joining
For experienced hires: technical and managerial interviews with the business that's hiring
looks_for: Strong technical foundations and conceptual clarity in your discipline
Energy, commitment and a passion for excellence
Safety-first thinking on sites and in plants
Willingness to work at project sites across India
questions: Tell me about a project or internship where something went wrong on the ground. What did you do?
Describe a time you worked in a team with a tight deadline and limited resources.
Tell me about a time you noticed a safety risk or a quality problem and spoke up.
Tell me about something you learned outside your syllabus because a project needed it.
Explain the difference between working stress design and limit state design, and why design codes use safety factors.
How would you check that concrete poured on site will reach its design strength?
Explain how a three-phase induction motor starts, and why starting current matters.
Walk me through how you'd choose a material for a pressure vessel or a heavy fabricated part.
A construction project is running two weeks behind schedule. How would you recover time without compromising safety?
Explain the critical path method and how you'd use it to plan a project.
Walk me through your final-year project: the problem, your part in it, and what you'd do differently.
How would you estimate the quantity of steel needed for a simple building frame? Talk me through your approach.
Why L&T, and which of its businesses would you like to work in?
Are you willing to work at project sites or plants anywhere in India, including remote locations?
Where do you see yourself five years after joining as a trainee?
tips: Revise your core subjects deeply; L&T's careers site says it looks for conceptual clarity, not just marks.
Know your final-year project and internships in detail, including the calculations and what didn't work.
Read about L&T's businesses on its website and be ready to say which one interests you and why.
Give an honest answer on site postings; projects can be far from cities, and interviewers want to see you've thought it through.
Expect a health examination before joining, which L&T's careers site notes for GETs.

body.name: Lenskart
rounds: Recruiter screen or campus shortlisting
Coding or problem-solving round for technology roles
System design or project deep dive for experienced engineers
Case, analytics or role-play round for business, retail and store roles (often)
Hiring manager round
HR round
looks_for: Speed and a willingness to experiment
Learning quickly from experiments that fail
Care for the customer across the app, website and stores
Comfort with retail data: footfall, conversion, returns, repeat purchase
questions: Tell me about an experiment you ran that failed. What did you learn, and what did you do next?
Describe a time you moved quickly to ship something. How did you keep the quality acceptable?
Tell me about a time you took ownership of a result that wasn't formally yours.
Tell me about a time you handled a difficult customer face to face.
How would you design a virtual try-on feature that shows frames on a customer's face through the phone camera?
A customer orders glasses online with a prescription. Walk me through the systems needed to make and deliver them.
Store sales in one city are flat while online sales there keep growing. How would you investigate?
How would you decide where to open the next few stores in a city?
How would you reduce returns from customers whose glasses don't fit or don't suit them?
How would you keep inventory accurate across warehouses, stores and the website?
A customer in a store is unsure about spending more on lenses. How would you help them choose without pushing?

For business cases, use retail metrics: footfall, conversion, average order value, repeat purchase and returns.
Show speed with judgement: what you'd test small first, and how you'd know to scale it.
For tech roles, think about performance on low-cost phones and patchy networks.

body.name: LTM (formerly LTIMindtree)
rounds: Campus drive, off-campus registration or online application
Online assessment: aptitude, reasoning, English and coding (often)
Technical interview on fundamentals, your coding approach and your projects
For experienced roles: one or two technical rounds, then a manager discussion
HR interview
looks_for: Data, cloud or AI basics for newer roles
A clear explanation of your own projects
questions: Tell me about yourself and the project you're proudest of.
Tell me about a time you kept going on something because you believed in why it mattered.
Tell me about a time you noticed someone on your team was having a hard time. What did you do?
Tell me about something new you taught yourself because you expected to need it.
Tell me about a result you delivered that someone else could measure.
Explain the difference between an array and a linked list, and when you'd choose each.
What is an index in a database, and when can adding one make things slower?
How would you design a simple link-shortening service: what would you store, and how would lookups work?
What is the difference between Git merge and rebase, and why do teams use pull requests?
What does a REST API do, and what do the common HTTP methods mean?
Your code passes on your machine but fails in the build pipeline. What do you check?

Why LTM, and what do you know about the industries it works in?
What would you like to be working on two years from now?

Practise coding in timed conditions in one language, and explain your approach before you write code.
Prepare a short story for each published value; 'Be future-ready' and 'Deliver impact' suit learning and project stories.
Read a recent case study or press release in an industry you like, so 'why us' sounds specific.

body.name: MakeMyTrip
rounds: Recruiter or HR screen, or campus shortlisting for graduate roles
Online test or coding round for engineering roles (often)
One or two technical rounds on problem-solving, data structures and your projects
System design for experienced engineers
Case or functional round for product, analytics and business roles
Hiring manager and HR round
looks_for: Understanding travellers: price, trust, choice and convenience
Designing for spiky demand around holidays, long weekends and sales
Thinking about partners (hotels, airlines) as well as customers
Ownership and a drive for results
questions: Tell me about a time you turned an unhappy customer or user into a satisfied one.
Describe a time you improved a product or process step by step rather than all at once.
Tell me about a time you worked with a partner or another team whose goals were different from yours.
Tell me about a deadline you nearly missed. What did you do?
How would you design flight search that pulls fares from many airlines and returns results quickly?
Two users try to book the last room in a hotel at the same moment. How would you stop it being sold twice?
A fare shown on the search page changes by the time the user reaches payment. How would you reduce this and handle it when it happens?
Hotel bookings in Goa fell sharply last week compared with the same week last year. How would you investigate?
How would you decide which hotels to show first for a search in Jaipur?
How would you estimate the number of hotel room-nights booked in Goa during December?
How would you design the refund journey for cancelled flights so customers stay informed at every step?
Why MakeMyTrip? Tell me about a trip you booked online and what you'd improve in that experience.
Which would you rather work on, flights, hotels or holidays, and why?
Where do you see yourself in five years, and how does this role help you get there?
tips: Search for a flight and a hotel on MakeMyTrip and Goibibo, go up to the payment page, and note where a traveller might hesitate.
Travel demand is seasonal: bring festivals, long weekends and holiday seasons into case and design answers.
In design questions, remember third-party suppliers: airline and hotel systems can be slow, fail or change prices.
For analytics roles, practise breaking a drop down by city, device, channel, and supply as well as demand.

body.name: Maruti Suzuki
rounds: Online application on the careers site, or campus shortlisting
Written or online test on aptitude and core engineering (often, for graduate roles)
Technical interview on core subjects, projects and internships
HR interview on fit, mobility and expectations
For experienced hires: technical and functional interviews with the hiring department
looks_for: Strong fundamentals in your engineering discipline
Shop-floor problem-solving on quality, cost, delivery and safety
Customer focus, from the showroom to after-sales service
Discipline and teamwork in a manufacturing setting
Willingness to take on challenges and grow with responsibility
Openness and respect for every voice, which the careers site describes as part of its culture
questions: Tell me about a time you found and fixed a small problem before it became a big one.
Describe a time you worked with people at different levels, such as technicians and managers, on one problem.
Tell me about a time you followed a process strictly even when a shortcut was tempting.
Tell me about a time you received critical feedback. What did you change?
Explain kaizen, and how you'd apply continuous improvement on an assembly line.
Explain just-in-time inventory, and what can go wrong with it when a supplier is late.
Warranty claims for one part on a car model are rising. How would you investigate?
How does a factory-fitted CNG car differ from a petrol one, and what are the key safety points?
Customers at a service workshop complain about long waiting times. How would you improve their experience?
Explain the difference between spot welding and arc welding, and where each is used in making a car.
How would you increase car sales in rural areas where many buyers are first-time owners?
Walk me through your final-year project and what you'd do differently today.
Why Maruti Suzuki?
Are you comfortable working in a plant, including shift work, if the role needs it?
Where do you see yourself in five years?

Bring examples of discipline and teamwork from projects, internships or sport.

body.name: Mastercard
rounds: Online application; some technology and early-careers roles include an online assessment
Recruiter screen on your background and interest in the role
Interviews with the hiring manager and team, often mixing technical or functional and behavioural questions
A case study, coding exercise or presentation for some roles
A final conversation with a senior leader for some roles
looks_for: Think big and bold; innovate with intention
Say what you mean; bring in different perspectives
Learn and pivot; own the outcome
Decency: doing the right thing with customers and each other
Thinking critically and bringing structure to complexity
questions: Tell me about a time you said what you meant, even though it was uncomfortable.
Tell me about a time you brought in someone with a different view and it improved the result.
Describe a time priorities changed suddenly. How did you adapt?
Tell me about a time you did the right thing when nobody would have noticed otherwise.
Tell me about a skill you're still developing. How are you working on it?
Tell me about a project where you owned the outcome from start to finish.
How would you design a service that lets a merchant accept card payments from many countries in different currencies?
Explain the roles of the issuer, the acquirer and the card network in a card payment.
What is a chargeback, and how would you help a merchant reduce disputes?

Why Mastercard, and what draws you to payments?
Which part of the Mastercard Way fits how you like to work, and which would stretch you?
What would you like to know about how this team measures success?

Show how you think, not just what you achieved: talk through the options you weighed and why you chose one.
Map your stories to Create value, Grow together and Move fast before the interview.
Know the card payment terms: issuer, acquirer, authorisation, clearing, settlement and chargeback.
For technical roles, expect questions on security and data protection; card data handling is tightly regulated.
If a skill is still developing, say so and show what you're doing to build it.

body.name: McKinsey
rounds: Problem-solving assessment (a digital game)
First round: case interviews with a personal experience interview
Final round: more case and personal experience interviews
questions: Tell me about a time you persuaded someone who disagreed with you.
Our client's profits fell 15% this year. How would you work out why?
Tell me about a time you led a team through a difficult situation.
Tell me about a time you set yourself an ambitious goal and kept going when it got hard.
Tell me about a time you brought together people with different views and made sure everyone was heard.
Tell me about a time you pushed for a change that others were comfortable without.
A regional airline is thinking about starting flights to a new country. How would you decide whether it should?
How would you estimate the number of fuel stations needed in Bengaluru? Talk me through your numbers.
A hospital wants to cut waiting times in its emergency department. How would you structure the problem?
Your client's revenue is growing, but its market share is falling. What does that tell you, and what would you look at next?
If a store's costs are 80% of its revenue, and revenue rises 8% while costs rise 12%, what happens to its profit margin? Talk me through it.

Why McKinsey, and why consulting rather than a role in industry?
Which industry or kind of problem would you most like to work on here, and why?
tips: Structure every case answer out loud before you solve it.
Prepare one deep story per personal experience theme; they'll probe it for 10–15 minutes.
Do case maths out loud with round numbers, say the units, and sanity-check the answer against the real world.
End each case with a clear recommendation, the main risk and what you'd check next, even if you haven't covered everything.
In the personal experience interview, choose stories where you personally made the difference; expect questions on what you thought, said and did at each step.
Practise with a partner who changes the facts mid-case, so a new question or chart doesn't throw you.

body.name: Meesho
rounds: Online coding test (for many engineering roles)
Problem-solving / data structures interviews
Low-level design or machine coding round
System design (for experienced roles)
Hiring manager round
HR or culture conversation
looks_for: Putting users first: buyers, sellers and delivery partners
Speed: shipping a first version fast and improving it
Acting like an owner of the outcome
Thinking big and long term, not only about the next quarter
Starting from the problem before the solution
Keeping costs low so the product stays affordable

Describe a time you put your company's or team's goal ahead of your own project.
Tell me about a time you spoke up because you thought a plan was wrong.
Tell me about a decision you got wrong. How did you find out, and what did you change?
How would you design a catalogue upload flow for small sellers who list products from their phones?
How would you recommend products to buyers who are new to online shopping and browse in their own language?
Returns are high in one clothing category. How would you reduce them without hurting sales?
How would you keep infrastructure costs low for a service with heavy traffic and low-value orders?
How would you design an API and app to work well on slow mobile networks and low-end phones?
How would you detect sellers listing fake or misleading products across a very large catalogue?
Estimate how many new sellers could be brought onto the platform from one textile hub, such as Surat, in a year.
Why Meesho? What do you understand about the buyers and sellers it serves?
Are you comfortable building for users whose lives are very different from yours? How would you learn about them?
tips: Keep Meesho's users in mind: buyers watching every rupee and sellers running small businesses. Bring them into design and product answers.
Practise low-level design: clear classes and interfaces and a working demo within the time.
Treat cost as a design constraint; cost per order matters a lot for a marketplace built around low prices.
Use the app as a buyer before the interview, and look at the seller side if you can, so you can talk about real flows.

body.name: Meta
rounds: Recruiter call
Technical screen (two coding problems)
Onsite loop: coding, system or product design, and a behavioral interview
looks_for: Impact: what changed because of your work
Be direct and respect your colleagues

Design a feature that helps people in a WhatsApp group plan an event together.

In design rounds, start with requirements and scale, then spend your time on the hardest parts rather than drawing every box.

body.name: Microsoft
rounds: Recruiter screen

Final 'as appropriate' interview with a senior leader

body.name: Morgan Stanley

body.name: Mphasis
rounds: Campus drive, online application or referral

body.name: Netflix

Technical or functional interviews

body.name: NHS

Pre-employment checks, such as references, occupational health and criminal record checks

looks_for: The employer's own values, often listed in the job advert
Safe practice: knowing your limits, escalating concerns and following guidance
Specific examples showing what you did and what you learned
questions: Tell me about a time you put a patient's or service user's needs first when it was difficult to do so.
Describe a time you protected someone's dignity in a situation where that was hard.
Tell me about a time you raised a concern about safety or the quality of care.
Tell me about a mistake you made at work or on placement. What did you do, and what did you learn?
Describe a time you worked with colleagues from other professions to improve someone's care or experience.
Tell me about a time you had several urgent tasks at once. How did you decide what to do first?

What does safeguarding mean in your role, and what would you do if you suspected abuse?
Talk me through how you would work out a drug dose from a prescription, and the checks you'd make before giving it.

International applicants: check your profession's registration steps early; the employer's interview is only one part of the process.

body.name: NTT DATA
rounds: Online application, with an online aptitude or coding test for some graduate roles
Recruiter screen on your background, career goals and fit for the role
Technical interview or assessment: a live discussion, a case-based conversation or an online test
Hiring manager interview on communication, adaptability, collaboration and client work

Steps vary by business unit, location and role, so read the job post closely and plan for each stage it names.

body.name: NVIDIA
rounds: Online application; NVIDIA suggests applying to the few roles that best match your background
Phone interviews with a recruiter, the hiring manager or engineers
Coding exercise for some technical roles, often on HackerRank
Virtual or in-person interviews: one-on-one, small-group or panel, usually 30–60 minutes each

looks_for: Intellectual Honesty: seek truth, learn from mistakes, share learnings
One Team: do what's best for the company
Deep knowledge of your area, from computer architecture to deep learning
Clear reasoning out loud on technical problems
Projects that show you've applied your skills, not only studied them

For a coding exercise, practise writing tested, readable code in a browser-based editor under time limits.
Prepare one project in depth with its numbers: speed-ups, utilisation, accuracy, area or power.

body.name: Nykaa

Final HR conversation

body.name: Ola

body.name: Oracle
rounds: Online application and a recruiter or HR screen
Online test for many campus and early-career roles: aptitude, coding and computer science basics
One or two technical interviews: data structures, databases and SQL, operating systems, and your projects
Hiring manager interview on past work, design and how you'd fit the team

Willingness to learn large, mature codebases

Why Oracle, and which part of its business (database, cloud or applications) interests you most?

For campus roles, practise aptitude and coding questions under time limits before the online test.

body.name: OYO

body.name: PayPal
