body.name: Qualcomm
rounds: Online application; a recruiter may reach out to discuss the role
Online test for many campus roles: aptitude and technical questions in your stream, sometimes coding
Two or more technical interviews: C and embedded systems, OS concepts, digital design or wireless basics, depending on the team
Hiring manager interview on your projects and fit with the team
HR discussion
looks_for: Strong C programming and embedded fundamentals for software roles
Digital design, verification or physical design depth for hardware roles
Wireless and signal processing basics for modem and systems roles
Explaining how your projects work, down to the details
questions: Tell me about a time you worked with a customer, partner or another team you didn't manage to fix a problem.
Tell me about a time you were relentless about getting something to work.
Tell me about a time you turned a difficult problem into an opportunity to try something new.
Tell me about a time you raised a concern because something didn't seem right.
Explain what the volatile keyword does in C and when you'd need it in embedded code.
What happens when an interrupt fires on a microcontroller, and what should an interrupt handler avoid doing?
Explain the difference between a mutex and a semaphore, with an example from an operating system or driver.
A device occasionally reboots in the field but never on your desk. How would you debug it?
Explain what OFDM is and why mobile networks use it.
How would you reduce the power a phone's modem or camera pipeline uses without hurting the user experience?
Explain the difference between synchronous and asynchronous resets, and when you'd use each.
Walk me through how an image goes from a phone's camera sensor to a saved photo.
Tell me about yourself and the project you're most proud of.
Why Qualcomm, and which technology area (modems, Snapdragon, automotive or IoT) interests you most?
tips: Revise C thoroughly: pointers, memory layout, bit manipulation, volatile, structures and padding; these come up often for software roles.
Know your stream's core subjects well: for electronics roles, digital design, signals and systems, and communication basics.
Be ready to explain your project at the level of registers, interfaces or algorithms, not just the outcome.
Qualcomm's values include Win together and Do the right thing; prepare a story for each.

body.name: Razorpay
rounds: Recruiter screen
Coding or machine coding round
System design (for experienced roles)
Hiring manager and culture round
looks_for: Using AI well in everyday work, which its careers page calls the 'AI Edge'
questions: Tell me about a production issue you owned. What did you change afterwards?
How would you design a payment retry system that never charges a customer twice?
Why Razorpay?
Tell me about a time you challenged the way your team had always done something.
Describe a time you shared bad news early with a customer or your team. Why then?
Tell me about a time you had to move fast without cutting a corner that mattered.
What is an idempotency key, and how would you use one in a payments API?
How would you design webhooks that tell merchants about payment events reliably?
How would you build daily reconciliation between your payment records and a bank's settlement file?
UPI success rates for one bank drop sharply at noon. What do you do?
Why should money be stored as whole numbers in the smallest unit, such as paise, rather than as floating-point numbers?
Walk me through how you use AI tools in your everyday work, and how you check what they produce.
A small online seller gave up halfway through setting up payments. How would you improve onboarding for sellers like them?
Which Razorpay product would you most like to work on, and what do you know about the businesses that use it?
tips: Payments care about correctness: talk about idempotency, retries and failure modes.
Razorpay says its interviews check for its six core values; prepare a short story for each, especially Customer First and Transparency.
Its careers page lists 'AI Edge' rounds on using AI in your work; bring a concrete example, including how you checked the output.
In design rounds, walk through failure cases out loud: timeouts, duplicate requests, a bank that replies late.
Know how a UPI or card payment flows between customer, merchant, payment gateway and bank before you go in.

body.name: Revolut
rounds: Recruiter or introductory call on your background and motivation
Online test or take-home task for many roles
Skills interview with the team on your experience and technical or functional depth
Problem-solving or case interview, often with numbers and a recommendation
Final interview with a senior team member for some roles
looks_for: Ownership: driving work to a result without waiting to be told
Speed with quality: moving quickly without cutting corners on risk or customers
Structured problem-solving and comfort with numbers
High standards and a habit of pushing for a better result
For risk, fraud and compliance roles: sound judgement on financial crime and regulation
questions: Tell me about the achievement you're proudest of. What exactly did you do, and how did you measure it?
Tell me about a time you delivered something much faster than people expected.
Tell me about a time you refused to settle for 'good enough' and pushed for a better result.
Describe a time you dug into data to find the root cause of a problem everyone else had explained away.
Tell me about a time you failed at something important. What did you change afterwards?
How would you design a system that stops card fraud in real time without blocking too many good customers?
A customer says money left their account for a payment they didn't make. Walk me through how you'd handle it.
How would you make sure a money transfer is never processed twice, even if the app retries the request?
How would you estimate how many people in Bengaluru might use a multi-currency travel card in a year?
Which metrics would you track for a new savings feature in a banking app, and what would make you change course?
What is transaction monitoring, and how would you cut false alerts without missing true cases of money laundering?
Why Revolut, and which part of the product would you most like to work on?
Which Revolut feature would you improve, and how would you know your change worked?
This role moves fast and asks a lot. Why does that kind of environment suit you?
tips: Bring numbers to every story: what changed, by how much and how quickly.
Practise a structured case answer out loud: clarify the goal, break the problem down, estimate, then recommend.
Use the app or read about its features, and come with one specific, realistic idea for improving a part of it.
For engineering roles, practise explaining payments trade-offs: consistency, retries, idempotency and audit trails.
Expect pushback on your answers; defend your reasoning calmly, and change your view if you're given a better fact.
The stages vary by team, so ask the recruiter what each interview will cover and prepare for that.

body.name: Salesforce
rounds: Recruiter screen
Hiring manager interview
Technical or functional panel
A presentation or case in some roles
looks_for: Real examples that match the job description's requirements
questions: Tell me about a time you turned around an unhappy customer.
How have you built trust with a team that was new to you?
Tell me about something new you introduced at work.
Tell me about a time you had to choose between hitting a target and doing what was right for the customer.
Tell me about a deal, project or launch that didn't go to plan. What did you learn?
What is a CRM, and how would you explain its value to a small business owner?
Salesforce runs many customers on shared infrastructure. How would you stop one customer's data or load from affecting another's?
How would you design a system that alerts a sales team when a big account shows signs it might leave?
Pitch a Salesforce product to me as if I lead sales at a retail company. Then handle my objection that it's too expensive.
A customer's integration with another system started failing after a release. How would you work out where the problem is?
On a platform like Salesforce, when would you build with point-and-click tools such as flows, and when would you write code?
Why Salesforce? Which of its core values matters most to you, and why?
Which Salesforce product, such as Slack or Tableau, would you most like to work on, and what would you improve?
tips: Connect your stories to Salesforce's core values.
Prepare stories in a clear situation, action and result shape; Salesforce says to expect behavioural, competency-based and situational questions.
Read the job description line by line and match a past example to each main requirement.
Learn the basics on Trailhead, Salesforce's free learning site, so you can talk about its products in your own words.
For a presentation round, keep it short, tie it to the customer's problem and leave time for questions and objections.
Expect virtual interviews to be on camera, and plan for an on-site interview before any offer.

body.name: Samsung
rounds: Online application or campus drive
Online coding test for software roles; candidates commonly report it rewards fully correct, well-tested solutions
Technical screening in digital electronics or your stream for some hardware and VLSI roles
One or two technical interviews: data structures, algorithms, operating systems, networks and your projects
For experienced roles, a deeper interview on the team's domain, such as Android, multimedia, modem, AI or chip design
HR round on motivation and teamwork
looks_for: Correct, working code and careful handling of edge cases
Solid computer science or electronics fundamentals
Depth in the team's domain: Android, multimedia, networks, AI or chip design
questions: Tell me about a time you kept improving something that already worked because you knew it could be better.
Tell me about a time you had to adapt quickly to a big change in a project.
Tell me about a time you worked with people from another country or culture on a shared goal.
Tell me about a time you submitted work with a bug you'd missed. What did you change in how you test?
How do you make sure your code handles edge cases before you submit it in a timed coding test?
Explain BFS and DFS, and describe a situation where you'd pick each.
Explain virtual memory and paging, and what happens on a page fault.
Explain how an Android app's activity lifecycle works, and describe a bug that comes from handling it badly.
How would you reduce the battery drain of a feature that runs in the background on a phone?
How would you design the software update system for millions of TVs or phones so a bad update can't break them all?
What is a memory leak in C or C++, and how would you find one in a device that runs for weeks?
How would you design a smart-home system that lets a phone control appliances from different makers?
Explain the difference between a latch and a flip-flop, and why designs usually prefer flip-flops.
Tell me about yourself and your strongest technical project.
Why Samsung, and which product or research area would you like to work on?
tips: Practise solving one hard problem completely in a timed setting, with your own test cases; candidates commonly report that partial solutions score poorly.
For software tests, revise graph search, recursion with backtracking and simulation-style problems, which candidates often mention.
Know the product side, from Galaxy phones and TVs to SmartThings and semiconductors, and connect your interest to one area.
Samsung lists five core values, including Excellence and Co-prosperity; have a story about teamwork and one about improving quality.
Prepare to explain your projects in depth, especially the code you wrote yourself.

body.name: SAP
rounds: Application review by the recruiting team
Online test for many campus and early-career roles: coding and aptitude
Technical interviews, often one or two: coding, computer science fundamentals and your projects
Hiring manager interview on your experience, motivation and fit with the team
HR discussion and offer
looks_for: Strong fundamentals: data structures, object-oriented design, databases and operating systems
Understanding of how businesses run: orders, invoices, stock, payroll
Building reliable, secure software for business customers
Working well across teams and countries
Curiosity and willingness to learn new tools, including cloud and AI
Honesty about what you know and don't know
questions: Tell me about a time you had to understand how a business process worked before you could build software for it.
Tell me about a time you worked with a teammate in another country or time zone. What made it work?
Tell me about a commitment to a teammate or customer that became hard to keep. What did you do?
Tell me about a piece of feedback that changed how you work.
Explain what an ERP system does, using a company that sells and ships products as your example.
How would you design an order-to-cash flow, from a customer placing an order to the company receiving payment?
What's the difference between a process and a thread, and when would you use multiple threads?
Explain how a database index speeds up queries, and what it costs.
A customer says month-end reports in their finance system have become very slow. How would you investigate?
What changes when a company moves a large business application from its own servers to the cloud? Talk me through the main risks.
Walk me through your best project: what you built, the hardest bug and what you'd do differently.
Why SAP, and which of its products or business areas interests you most?
SAP's customers are mostly businesses, not consumers. Why does building that kind of software appeal to you?
Where do you see yourself in five years?
tips: Learn how a business runs day to day: a sale, an invoice, a stock movement, a payslip. SAP's software is built around these flows.
Revise core subjects (data structures, OOP, databases, operating systems, networks); campus technical rounds commonly test them.
Know one project end to end, including design choices and how you tested it; interviewers often go deep on one project.
SAP's careers site prefers applications in English and lets you apply to several roles; pick the ones that genuinely match your skills.
If you're early in your career, look at the academies on SAP's careers site; each has its own focus, such as product and engineering or customer success.

body.name: State Bank of India
rounds: Online application against an official notification on SBI's careers page
Phase I: an online preliminary exam (objective), used to shortlist for the main exam
Phase II: an online main exam; for officers it usually includes objective and descriptive tests
Officers, Phase III: usually a psychometric test, a group exercise and a personal interview
Clerks: a test of the chosen local language for candidates who didn't study it at school, as the notification sets out
Document verification and a medical check before joining
Specialist Cadre Officers: separate notifications by post; selection varies, often shortlisting and an interview
looks_for: In the interview: clear communication, awareness of banking and the economy, and a sound reason for choosing SBI
In the group exercise: contributing ideas, listening and helping the group reach a conclusion
Willingness to work in any branch, including rural and semi-urban ones
questions: Tell me about a time you helped someone who was unfamiliar with a process, such as filling in a form or using an app.
Describe a time you led a group without being formally in charge.
Tell me about a time you stayed polite with someone who was being rude or unreasonable.
Tell me about a time you chose honesty even though it was the harder option.
What is financial inclusion, and how does a bank like SBI support it?
Explain the repo rate and the cash reserve ratio, and how changes in them affect lending.
A farmer in your branch area is struggling to repay a crop loan after a poor monsoon. What would you consider?
How would you increase the use of digital banking among older customers at a rural branch?
A customer says they shared an OTP on a phone call and money has left their account. What would you do?
What is a non-performing asset, and why does it matter to a public-sector bank?
Group exercise practice: should India move towards a fully cashless economy? Give your view and a counterpoint.
Explain one recent RBI or government step in banking and what it means for ordinary customers.
Tell me about yourself and why you want to join SBI.
Why a public-sector bank rather than a private bank?
You may be posted to a remote rural branch far from home. How do you feel about that?
tips: Read the official notification for your cycle on SBI's careers page: stages, eligibility and dates change, and the notification is the authority.
SBI says it informs shortlisted candidates individually and publishes only roll or registration numbers; ignore any message asking for money.
For the interview, prepare to talk about your own background (home district, degree subjects, hobbies), as panels often start there.
In the group exercise, make a clear point early, build on others' points, help the group summarise, and don't talk over people.
Know SBI's core values (Service, Transparency, Ethics, Politeness, Sustainability) and have one example for each from your life.
Follow banking and economy news daily: RBI policy, government schemes, digital payments and financial inclusion.

body.name: ServiceNow
rounds: Recruiter screen after an application review
Online coding assessment for many engineering roles
Technical interviews, often two or three: coding, problem solving and system design for experienced roles
A presentation for some roles, such as pre-sales and consulting
Hiring manager interview on past work and values
Team debrief and decision
looks_for: Working as one team across engineering, product and sales
Drive to learn, with humility about what you don't know
Understanding of how large organisations run IT, HR and service work
questions: Tell me about a time you went beyond what a customer or user expected.
Tell me about a time you helped a teammate succeed, even though it wasn't your task.
Tell me about a time you were wrong about something technical. How did you find out, and what did you change?
Tell me about a time you helped someone new to the team feel included.
What is IT service management? Explain the difference between an incident and a problem to a new joiner.
How would you design a ticketing system that routes each request to the right team automatically?
How would you design approval workflows, such as a laptop request needing a manager's sign-off, so steps can change without new code?
A workflow that ran fine yesterday is now timing out for one large customer. How would you find the cause?
How would you make search fast across millions of records in a web application?
Walk me through how you'd present our platform to a customer's head of IT whose request process is slow and manual.
Explain REST APIs, and how you'd connect two business systems so their data stays in sync.
Why ServiceNow? What do you think its platform does for the companies that use it?
ServiceNow's purpose is to make the world work better for everyone. What would that mean in the work you'd do here?
What questions do you have for us about the team or the role?
tips: ServiceNow says interviews, tests and technical challenges must be done without AI help unless it tells you otherwise, so practise solving problems on your own.
Learn the basics of IT service management (incidents, requests, changes) so you can talk about the problems the platform solves.
For a presentation, start with the customer's problem and the outcome, then show how the solution gets there.
Prepare a story about customer impact and one about helping your team; interviewers commonly probe both.
ServiceNow University offers no-cost courses and certifications on the platform; a short course can help you talk about it with confidence.

body.name: Shell
rounds: Online application
Online assessments, often job simulations and questions about how you work
Recorded video interview
Final virtual assessment: a case study shared in advance, a short presentation and questions from assessors
looks_for: Analysing a situation and proposing practical solutions
Drive to achieve, and learning from feedback
Working well with people from different backgrounds
Honesty, integrity and respect for people
Understanding of the energy transition and commercial trade-offs
questions: Tell me about a time you analysed a messy situation and proposed a solution others adopted.
Tell me about an achievement you worked hard for. What drove you?
Tell me about a time you worked in a team of people from different backgrounds. How did you make it work?
Tell me about feedback that was hard to hear and what you changed because of it.
Tell me about a time you stopped or questioned something because it didn't look safe or right.
How would you decide whether a company should invest in a new solar or wind project? Talk me through the factors.
Fuel sales at a group of service stations have dropped. How would you find out why?
In two minutes, explain what the energy transition means for an energy company.
A pump at a plant keeps failing earlier than expected. How would you find the root cause?
You get a business case two days before a meeting. How would you prepare a five-minute recommendation?
A project is behind schedule. How would you balance safety, cost and time to get it back on track?
Why Shell, and why a career in energy?
Which part of Shell's business interests you most, and why?
tips: In a case presentation, give your recommendation first, then the reasons, the risks and the next steps.
Expect follow-up scenarios after a presentation; candidates commonly report assessors changing the facts to see how you adapt.
Prepare stories that show how you analyse problems, what you've achieved and how you work with others.
Read about Shell's businesses and its plans for lower-carbon energy so you can discuss them in your own words.
Test your camera, microphone and connection before any virtual interview or assessment.

body.name: Shopify
rounds: Recruiter screen
'Life story' conversation about your path and choices
Technical interviews, often pair programming
Team or lead interview
looks_for: Impact, readiness, trust, engagement and self-awareness (the traits Shopify's engineering blog says the Life Story looks for)
questions: Walk me through your life story: the big choices and why you made them.
Tell me about a time things changed fast at work. What did you do?
Who are Shopify's merchants, and what would you build for them?
Tell me about one of your bruises: a decision that went wrong and what you learned from it.
Tell me about the achievement you're proudest of. What impact did it have, and on whom?
Tell me about a time you taught yourself something hard because the work needed it.
Walk me through a project you know well: the architecture, the trade-offs you made and what you'd do differently.
In a pair-programming session, how do you share your thinking with your partner? Talk me through how you'd start a new task.
How would you design a checkout that keeps working when a merchant's flash sale brings ten times the usual traffic?
A merchant says orders stopped appearing in their admin an hour ago. How would you investigate?
How would you design inventory tracking that keeps stock counts right across an online store and a physical shop?
Why Shopify, and what does making commerce better for everyone mean to you?
What do you want to learn in your next role, and how will you know you're growing?
tips: For the life-story round, explain why you made each choice, not just what you did.
Before the Life Story, list your turning points, proudest wins and hardest moments; Shopify says it wants to hear about the trophies and the bruises.
In pair programming, think aloud and ask your partner questions. Shopify's engineering blog says a well-reasoned incomplete solution beats a fragile finished one.
For the technical deep dive, pick a project with real business trade-offs rather than a solo side project, and treat it as a conversation.
Try the product as a merchant would, for example by setting up a test store, so you can talk about it from experience.

body.name: Siemens
rounds: Online application and CV screening
Online test or recorded video interview for some roles and graduate schemes
Technical interview on your discipline, projects and problem solving
Behavioural or HR interview on motivation, teamwork and fit
Assessment centre for graduate programmes, with several exercises
Final discussion and offer
looks_for: Solid fundamentals in your field: electrical, mechanical, software or automation
A practical, structured approach to solving problems
Responsibility for safety, quality and ethical conduct
Understanding of why the technology matters to the customer
Working well in diverse, international teams
questions: Tell me about a technical problem you solved in a project, lab or internship. How did you find the cause?
Tell me about a time you noticed a quality or safety risk. What did you do?
Tell me about a time you worked in a team with people from different disciplines or backgrounds.
Tell me about a time you had to learn a new tool or technology quickly.
What's a weakness you're working on, and how are you improving it?
Explain what a PLC does in a factory, and how it differs from an ordinary computer.
What is a digital twin, and how could a manufacturer use one?
A production line keeps stopping at the same station. How would you find out why?
How would you reduce the energy a large building uses, with sensors and controls?
Explain how a three-phase induction motor works, as you would to a first-year student.
Walk me through your final-year project: the goal, your design choices and the results.
Why Siemens, and which of its businesses interests you most?
Siemens works on digitalisation and sustainability. Which of these interests you most for your career, and why?
Are you open to working on customer sites or travelling for projects?
tips: Revise the core of your discipline; technical interviewers commonly go back to fundamentals from your degree.
Know one or two Siemens businesses relevant to your field and the problems they solve for customers.
Siemens' careers site welcomes AI for preparing, but not during live interviews or assessments; practise answering on your own.
For a graduate assessment centre, expect several exercises as well as interviews, and treat each as a fresh start.

body.name: Spotify
rounds: Recruiter call by video or phone
Interview with one or two team members (for engineers, often a technical or coding interview)
Final round with several people from across the business: technical depth, system design for experienced roles, and values
Decision and feedback from the recruiter
looks_for: Ownership and pride in what you deliver
The thinking behind your results, not just the results
questions: Tell me about a piece of work you're proud of. What was your part, and what did it achieve?
Tell me about a time plans changed suddenly. How did you adapt?
Tell me about a time you worked closely with people in other disciplines, such as design or data, to ship something.
Tell me about a goal you kept pushing towards even when it got hard.
Tell me about a time you tried a new approach that didn't work out. What did you learn?
How would you design a feature that builds a personalised playlist for each listener every week?
How would you make a song start playing quickly, even on a weak mobile connection?
How would you test whether a new home screen layout makes people listen more?
Explain the trade-offs of splitting a large app into many small services owned by different teams.
Play counts for new releases look too low on an artist dashboard. How would you work out whether the data or the product is wrong?
Walk me through a system or project you know well: the design, what broke and what you learned.
Why Spotify? How do you use it, and what would you change?
What do you want to learn here, and how does this role fit where you're heading?
tips: Spotify says it tells you who your interviewers are at each stage; look at their teams so your questions fit.
Make the things Spotify asks about easy to hear: shared values, ownership, adaptability, collaboration and drive. Prepare a story for each.
Explain the thinking behind your results, not just the results; Spotify says it wants to understand how you got there.
Technical interviews may use shared tools such as CoderPad; practise coding and explaining in a plain online editor.

body.name: Stripe
rounds: Recruiter screen
Technical screen with practical coding
Onsite: practical coding (debugging, building against an API), system design, and behavioral interviews
questions: Tell me about a bug you tracked down that others couldn't.
How would you design an API that lets businesses refund a payment safely?
Tell me about a time you did more for a user than your role asked.
Tell me about something you wrote, such as a design doc or post-mortem, that changed what your team did.
Tell me about a piece of work you're proud of for its craft, not only its result.
Tell me about a time you changed course because someone else's idea was better than yours.
What is idempotency, and how would you make a payment request safe to retry?
How would you design a system that delivers webhooks to merchants reliably, even when their servers are down?
You're handed an unfamiliar codebase and a failing test. Talk me through how you'd find the cause.
How would you design a ledger that records money moving between accounts so the books balance?
What makes an API pleasant for developers to integrate? Give examples of good and bad design.
How would you help a small online business reduce failed payments at checkout?
Why Stripe, and which of its products or users interest you most?
Which of Stripe's operating principles fits how you like to work, and which would stretch you most?
tips: Practise practical tasks (reading code, fixing bugs, calling an API), not just puzzles.
Talk about correctness: idempotency and failure modes matter in payments.
Stripe says it shares written guides before interviews; read yours closely, as it explains the format and how to prepare.
Stripe has written that engineers can use their own laptop and development environment; know your editor, tests and debugger well.
Try Stripe's API documentation and test mode before the interview so building against an API feels familiar.

body.name: Swiggy
rounds: Online coding assessment
Problem solving / data structures
Machine coding or low-level design
System design (for experienced roles)
Hiring manager round
looks_for: Always be Curious, Always be Learning
Move Fast, Break Barriers and Deliver Results
questions: How would you design order tracking for a food-delivery app?
Tell me about a time you shipped something fast. What trade-offs did you make?
Tell me about a feature you built that users loved.
Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision, said so, and then committed to it fully.
Describe a time you delivered something useful with fewer people, less time or less money than you wanted.
Tell me about feedback that was hard to hear. What did you change because of it?
How would you assign incoming orders to delivery partners in a busy area at dinner time?
How would you estimate the delivery time shown to a customer before they place an order?
How would you keep stock accurate in a quick-commerce app that serves customers from many small stores?
Payments in one city start failing during a cricket final. Walk me through your first 30 minutes.
Explain the trade-offs between polling, WebSockets and push notifications for live updates in a mobile app.
Repeat orders from new users in one city fell last month. How would you find out why?
Why Swiggy? Which of Swiggy's values fits how you like to work?
Which part of Swiggy (food delivery, Instamart or dining out) would you like to work on, and what would you improve first?
tips: Real-time systems (tracking, dispatch, ETAs) are favourite design topics.
Swiggy groups its published values into heart, head and hands; prepare a story each for consumer focus, founder mentality and disagree-and-commit.
For machine coding, get a working version running early, then refactor into clear classes, and leave time to walk the interviewer through it.
In design answers, cover everyone the system serves: customers, restaurant partners and delivery partners.
Mention cheap phones and patchy networks when you talk about the apps; it shows you're thinking about real users across India.

body.name: Tata Motors
rounds: Online application through the careers site, or campus shortlisting
Online test: for its early-career programme, the careers site lists aptitude and reasoning, basic maths, subject knowledge and general English
Technical interview on core engineering subjects, projects and internships
HR or managerial interview on fit, mobility and motivation
Background verification and a medical check-up before joining (listed for its early-career programme)
For experienced hires: technical and functional interviews with the hiring team
looks_for: Strong engineering fundamentals for design, manufacturing, quality and service roles
Interest in vehicles, electric mobility and connected technology
Shop-floor problem-solving on quality, cost and delivery
Customer focus, from fleet owners to car buyers
questions: Tell me about a time you improved a process, even slightly, during an internship or project.
Describe a time you had to find the root cause of a problem that kept coming back.
Tell me about a team project where members disagreed. How did you reach a decision?
Tell me about a time you took on something unfamiliar. How did you get up to speed?
Explain how a battery electric vehicle's powertrain differs from a diesel truck's.
What does a battery management system do, and why does thermal management matter in an EV?
A defect keeps appearing at one station on an assembly line. How would you find the root cause and stop it?
What does lean manufacturing mean to you? Explain one tool you've used or studied, such as kaizen, 5S or poka-yoke.
How would you reduce the total cost of owning a truck for a fleet owner?
Walk me through how you'd design a bracket that carries a load, from requirements to testing.
Sales of one car model are lower than expected in smaller towns. How would you investigate?
How would you plan the public charging needed for electric car owners in a city like Pune?
Why Tata Motors, and are you more interested in the commercial or the passenger vehicle side?
Are you willing to work at plants or in field roles in different parts of India?
Where do you see yourself five years from now?
tips: Revise your branch's core subjects; for EV roles add batteries, motors and power electronics.

turns.text: Thanks for making time today. To start, tell me about a time you used data to change a product decision.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: At Juniper Logistics most late deliveries came from one promise we showed at checkout. I built a delivery-time model, made the case to show a window instead of a date, and late deliveries fell 18% in two quarters.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Walk me through an A/B test you designed, and what you'd do differently next time.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We tested a delivery window against a single date. Cancellation rate was the main metric, conversion the guardrail, two weeks, split by city. Cancellations fell about 6% with no drop in conversion, so it shipped. Next time I'd run it a week longer to rule out a novelty effect.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How would you investigate a sudden drop in weekly bookings?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: First check it's real: tracking, a release, a holiday. Then split by platform, city and funnel step. At Fernway a drop like that was one Android release that broke the date picker.
